payload.answer: [hard] Every change carries a before/after measurement committed as evidence. A performance change with no number attached is not a performance change. [hard] Correctness is never traded for speed. All 7 gates stay green, including 100% branch coverage per layer -- a faster system that drops a job or double-counts spend is a regression regardless of the benchmark. [hard] The ledger stays append-only and the queue stays PostgreSQL; no caching layer that can serve stale budget data, since the budget brake is a safety mechanism and a stale read there spends real money. [hard] domain/ stays pure. [hard] No micro-optimisation without a measured win -- if it does not move a number, it does not land. This is a deliberate optimisation push, not licence to churn. [soft] Prefer pushing filters into SQL over adding indexes; prefer adding an index over adding a cache. [hard] Conventional Commits, feature branch into develop.

A committed benchmark harness that anyone can re-run, with baseline numbers recorded before any change. Claim-path budget checks no longer scan full project history -- demonstrated by a test with a large synthetic ledger where time stays flat as history grows, rather than by a stopwatch. build_app no longer re-applies migrations on every call. Each landed change names its measured improvement. All 7 gates green.

The largest measured defect is in the claim path. LedgerBudgetSource.current() calls all_for_project() and then filters IN PYTHON -- `for event in ...: if event.cycle != cycle: continue`. That is a full-history scan on every budget check, on every claim. greeter4 already carries 1,778 events; the scan grows without bound for the life of a project while the useful slice stays roughly constant. The database is already indexed for the fix -- event_kind on (project_id, kind, seq) exists and this path never reaches it, because the filtering never gets to SQL. A second, unlisted defect: build_app() creates a pool AND re-applies migrations on every call, so any command opening it repeatedly pays the migration machinery each time.

A measurement-first performance campaign across the vibey stack, executing runbook 13's Front 2 'orchestration hot paths' (items 5-8) rather than inventing a parallel agenda. Those items are already scoped: ledger scan elimination, claim batching, event-tail latency, connection discipline. Do not duplicate two things: doctor's sequential engine checks are a SEPARATE project already running, and runbook 13 Front 1 (test-suite parallelism, template databases) already shipped as PR #70.
